MO-2026-HB1696.s: The bill updates who can make burial or cremation choices for a person who dies, with a set order for family members and others to follow. It also lets funeral directors rely on the person who claims that right, and sets rules for notice, waiver, and disputes among equal family members. For residential camps, staff and volunteers age 18 or older must pass a criminal background check before they start, including sex offender and criminal record searches in Missouri and other states where they lived in the past five years. It was approved by the governor on July 13, 2026.

MO-2026-HB1825.s: The law changes how county salary commissions are made in Missouri. It removes the prosecuting attorney and the sheriff from the salary commission in nonchartered counties, except in counties with 150,000 to 200,000 people and in counties with part-time prosecuting attorneys, where those prosecutors still serve on the commission.

MO-2026-HB1827.s: Missouri would add licensed occupational therapists to the list of health care workers who can sign the medical statement needed for disabled license plates and placards. The change affects people who apply for these plates or placards and the therapists who may fill out the form. The bill was approved by the governor.

MO-2026-HB1871.s: The law changes several election rules in Missouri. It sets August 12 as Election Worker Appreciation Day, limits what a person can do with a candidate committee after registering as a lobbyist, and changes steps for county and other local bond filings. It also changes notice and newspaper posting rules for elections, including moving some notices to up to six weeks before the election.

MO-2026-HB1940.s: The law changes how election notices and other public notices must be published in newspapers. It moves some election notice deadlines, changes when and where notices must run, and allows some notices to be mailed to voters instead of published in some cases. It also shortens the time a newspaper must have been published before it can carry legal ads from three years to one year.

MO-2026-HB2002.s: The bill would set spending for the State Board of Education and the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education for July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. It covers money for school funding, pre-K grants, school meals, educator pay grants, and other agency programs. The governor vetoed part of the bill.

MO-2026-HB2003.s: The bill would set aside money for the Missouri Department of Higher Education and Workforce Development and its programs for July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. It covers grants, refunds, fund transfers, and aid programs for public colleges and students, including scholarships and workforce grants. The governor vetoed part of it on June 30, 2026.

MO-2026-HB2004.s: This bill would set aside state money for the Missouri Department of Revenue and the Department of Transportation for July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. It covers spending for fees, tax work, motor vehicle and driver licensing, legal services, and payments to cities, counties, ports, and other local governments. It also allows some money to be moved between certain funds and program areas.

MO-2026-HB2005.s: The bill would set spending for the Office of Administration, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Conservation, the Department of Public Safety, and the governor’s office for July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. It would also move money among some state funds and pay for state services, including information technology, planning, budgeting, and public safety work. The money comes from state funds named in the bill, including general revenue and other state accounts.

MO-2026-HB2006.s: The bill would set money for the Missouri Departments of Agriculture, Natural Resources, and Conservation, plus related programs, for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. It includes money for staff, grants, refunds, transfers between funds, and some building and road work, including the Clarendon Road move and the I-70 project. It also sets money for farm and food programs, veterinary student loans, and agricultural education. The governor vetoed part of the bill.

MO-2026-HB2007.s: This bill would set state money for the Missouri departments of Economic Development, Commerce and Insurance, and Labor and Industrial Relations for the year starting July 1, 2026, and ending June 30, 2027. It covers staff pay, office costs, grants, refunds, and money transfers between state funds. The listed uses include economic development, community programs, tourism, downtown projects, and labor-related work. It was vetoed in part by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2008.s: The bill would fund the Missouri Department of Public Safety and the Department of the National Guard for the state fiscal year starting July 1, 2026, and ending June 30, 2027. It includes money for grants, refunds, fund transfers, and programs such as fire, police, jail, school safety, drug task force, and victim services work. The governor vetoed part of the bill.

MO-2026-HB2009.s: The bill would set money for the Missouri Department of Corrections for the state fiscal year from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. It covers costs for prison staff, food service, building work, offender supervision, reentry programs, substance use treatment, and other department services. The bill passed the legislature and was later partly vetoed by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2010.s: Appropriates money for the Missouri Department of Mental Health, the Department of Health and Senior Services, and the Missouri Health Facilities Review Committee for July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. It sets funding for staff, services, refunds, grants, and fund transfers, including Medicaid-related payments and mental health programs. The bill was delivered to the governor and later vetoed in part.

MO-2026-HB2011.s: The bill would set aside state money for the Missouri Department of Social Services and its programs for the year from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. It also would move some money between certain state funds and pay for items like staff, grants, technology, audits, and help with Medicaid and child abuse work. The governor vetoed part of it.

MO-2026-HB2012.s: This bill would set state funding for Missouri’s top elected offices, the courts, the state public defender, and the General Assembly for the year starting July 1, 2026, and ending June 30, 2027. It includes money for office costs, election work, grants, refunds, fund transfers, and some one-time items for specific projects and programs. The bill also covers money for the Missouri Arts Council, Missouri Humanities Council, public broadcasting, and other state services that use these funds.

MO-2026-HB2013.s: The bill would set aside state money for real property leases, related services, utilities, furniture, building changes, and other expenses for Missouri state departments and programs from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. It also would move money among certain funds and provide funding for many state agencies, including education, revenue, public safety, corrections, health, and social services. The bill was approved by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2017.s: The bill would set aside money for capital projects and other work for several state departments, schools, and universities for July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. It includes funding for school facility work, higher education projects, airport improvements, and major road work on I-70, including $925,662,390 for that project. The bill was vetoed in part by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2019.s: This act was approved by the governor and sets state money for many departments and projects for the fiscal year from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. It funds work for education, natural resources, economic development, social services, public safety, conservation, and the National Guard, including building repairs, water and sewer projects, parks, roads, and public facilities. Many of the funds go to specific local projects, and some require a local match, which means the local group must help pay part of the cost.

MO-2026-HB2020.s: It would set state money for many departments and programs for July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. The funding covers things like grants, refunds, equipment, building work, and transfers between funds. It includes money for transportation, economic development, public safety, veterans’ homes, job centers, broadband, and state buildings.

MO-2026-HB2108.s: The law lets the governor sell or transfer certain state land in Cole County to the City of Jefferson. It also gives temporary construction easements, which are short-term rights to use land for building work, in several areas tied to that property. The measure became law after the governor approved it.

MO-2026-HB2292.s: The law adds training for certain child, adult, and animal welfare workers on how to spot and report abuse or neglect, including abuse of companion animals like dogs, cats, rabbits, and pet birds. It also creates a duty for some professionals and animal control staff to report suspected abuse across child, adult, and animal cases, with penalties for not reporting and some confidentiality for reporters. The law also requires reports to state leaders about call wait times and how often these cases are linked, and it was approved by the governor on July 13, 2026.

MO-2026-HB2397.s: The law changes how a public water supply district can be dissolved. It sets steps for filing in circuit court, notice, court review, and a vote by district voters, and it can require all debts to be paid before dissolution. It also lets a district board help pay for employee health, medical, or life insurance plans, with the insurance contract put out for bids at least every three years.

MO-2026-HB2474.s: Missouri’s law changes how some public projects can use design-build and progressive design-build contracts. It lowers the dollar limit for some noncivil projects from $7 million to $2.5 million, adds rules for progressive design-build work, and says local governments cannot use certain unrelated standards, like green building ratings or diversity goals, as a condition for those bids. It also lets the state purchasing office join certain buying agreements with other government groups and, in some cases, let local governments take part too.

MO-2026-HB2508.s: The law would let people search each series of a series LLC on the secretary of state’s business website by January 31, 2027. It also lets anyone ask the secretary of state for a certificate of good standing for a regular LLC or for an individual series, which is a paper saying the business exists and may do business in Missouri. It affects domestic and foreign LLCs and their series, and the bill was approved by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2576.s: The bill would create many new Missouri state designations, including awareness weeks and days, official titles for some places and symbols, and several memorial highways and bridges. It also names official items such as the state promotional song, mushroom, and a few local honors. The measure was approved by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2593.s: The bill changes several rules for Missouri military affairs. It would give contract bonus points to some Missouri veteran-owned businesses and set similar rules for service-disabled veteran businesses, with a 3 percent goal for some state contracts. It would also change pay and benefits for National Guard members on active duty, update reemployment and legal protections for some service members, and create or revise military relief and counterdrug programs and funds.

MO-2026-HB2636.s: The bill would set rules for mortgage changes and for some real estate deals in Missouri. It would require extra written notices and signed forms for people who buy homes to resell them, and it would give sellers a right to cancel in some cases if the notices are not given. It would also add protections for sale-leaseback deals, where a person sells a home and then rents it back, including a 30-day wait before closing and possible civil penalties. The mortgage part defines terms and sets rules for when a mortgage modification is covered.

MO-2026-HB2637.s: The measure would expand how Missouri tracks arrest, charge, and court records, and it would require more reporting to the state criminal record system. It would also let local prosecutors ask the attorney general for help in cases that cross more than one part of the state. For some juvenile cases and some law enforcement referrals, it sets new fingerprinting and reporting rules, including a 2028 date for certain referral reports. The bill was approved by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2818.s: The law changes the rules for when a city, town, or village can annex, or add, nearby unincorporated land. It sets new tests for what counts as “contiguous and compact,” adds special rules for some counties and certain cities, and changes the steps for notice, hearings, objections, and annexation by ordinance. It also lets challenges to an annexation under this section be brought within five years of the ordinance date.

MO-2026-HB2819.s: The bill lets sellers round the final total of a cash sale to the nearest five cents after items, discounts, and taxes are figured. It does not apply to credit, debit, or other noncash payments, and the sales tax still must be sent to the state based on the tax rules. The bill was approved by the governor.

MO-2026-HB2974.s: This bill would let some people who already hold a valid license from another state, a military branch, a U.S. territory, or Washington, D.C., apply for the same job license in Missouri with fewer extra steps. It also creates a multistate dietitian license compact, which lets qualifying dietitians practice across member states and helps military spouses and other licensed workers move more easily. The bill was approved by the Governor on July 13, 2026.

MO-2026-HR2.s: The House resolution would tell the Senate that the House took no motions to override the governor’s vetoes of several listed bills. It affects those vetoed bills and the House and Senate. It is a formal statement from the House, not a new law.

MO-2026-SB1000.s: The bill changes how the state tourism fund gets money. It would replace the current tourism-tax funding rules with money approved by lawmakers and with gifts, grants, and other donations from public or private sources. It was signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SB1002.s: The law changes election rules for school districts where most of the district is in St. Charles County. School board elections there must be held at the November general election, and board terms would be four years. Candidates may choose to list a party label next to their name on the ballot. Voter questions on new taxes, tax renewals or increases, and bond debt for those districts must also be placed on the November general election ballot.

MO-2026-SB1003.s: The bill would change several Missouri National Guard and veterans programs. It would update how aid from the Missouri Military Family Relief Fund is handled, add new Guard ribbons, and create a fund for money from federal asset forfeiture programs. It would also let the Guard help with cybersecurity work for state and local public agencies, schools, police, utilities, and critical infrastructure when asked by the Department of Public Safety.

MO-2026-SB1019.s: Becomes law and changes several health care rules in Missouri. It raises how much money certain municipal and hospital district hospitals can invest, and it lets those hospitals operate in some of the same areas as county hospitals and each other. It also creates a state Lyme disease program that requires a yearly report and asks state health officials to work with public colleges on disease tracking.

MO-2026-SB1033.s: Missouri SB 1033 became law and changes some air quality rules. It changes how money in certain natural resources funds can be moved to the state general fund, and it changes how some farm vehicles are treated under emissions inspection rules. It also says some cotton gin owners do not need to submit air dispersion modeling to get a construction permit if they meet the bill's limits on air pollution.

MO-2026-SB1085.s: The bill would bar public school and charter school staff from encouraging a minor student’s social transition, meaning a change in gender presentation or expression to be seen as a different sex. It would also require staff to notify a parent within 24 hours if a student asks to use a different pronoun, a different name, a restroom for the other sex, or a sports team for the other sex. The bill also sets rules for discipline, legal action, and court fees for violations.

MO-2026-SB1119.s: The bill creates a process for naming commissioners to a convention called under Article V of the U.S. Constitution. The Missouri General Assembly would appoint these commissioners, and a joint legislative committee would recommend names and rules for their work. The Legislature approved it and the governor signed it on July 13, 2026.

MO-2026-SB1135.s: This law creates a child support rule for some people convicted of driving while intoxicated or driving with too much alcohol in their blood when that conduct caused a parent or guardian’s death. If a surviving parent or guardian asks for it, a court can order the convicted person to pay child maintenance for the child, with payment timing adjusted if the person is jailed or otherwise confined. Any court award or car insurance payment tied to the death can reduce the order, but payments from the Crime Victims' Compensation Fund cannot.

MO-2026-SB1196.s: The bill would keep the Workforce Diploma Program in place past its current end date, so it could continue helping students earn a high school diploma and build job skills. It would also direct the state higher education agency to create a new funding plan for public colleges and technical schools, with testing and later approval steps before it can take effect. For the Fast Track Workforce Incentive Grant, it would raise the income limits for who can qualify and require training providers to have been legally open in Missouri for at least 12 months. It would also let the governor approve eligible workforce training programs for workforce Pell grants and move the Missouri Workforce Development Board to the higher education department.

MO-2026-SB1233.s: The bill changes Missouri rules for interior designers from registration to licensing and moves oversight to the state board for architects and related design fields. It adds two licensed interior designers to that board, changes education, training, and continuing education rules, and sets limits on who may take charge of technical interior design work. It also transfers the old interior design council's funds and makes licensed interior designers part of the group covered by a peer review liability rule.

MO-2026-SB1408.s: The bill would raise the top speed on rural interstates and freeways in Missouri from 70 to 75 miles per hour. It was signed by the governor, so it became law.

MO-2026-SB1421.s: This law changes several public safety rules in Missouri. It lets the Attorney General appoint investigators, raises some record request fees from $15 to $20, and changes how prosecuting attorneys are paid in different counties. It also lets school districts use school bus safety cameras if their board approves, with limits on how long unused images can be kept and how they can be used.

MO-2026-SB1442.s: The bill would change how Missouri schools teach and check early reading. It would require teacher training programs to use approved reading materials, add more support for teachers and tutoring, and create a statewide reading screener for students in grades 1-3. Schools would also give parents more guidance for helping children read at home, and some reading aid money could be used during school hours.

MO-2026-SB1534.s: The bill would change how some sales tax rules work in Missouri. It would keep credit card and debit card processing fees out of sales tax calculations, and businesses that charge those fees would have to tell customers about them. It would also make retail food sales exempt from state sales tax and send part of the state sales tax rate to the School District Trust Fund.

MO-2026-SB1553.s: Missouri’s bill would expand a sales tax break to cover critical materials and critical pharmaceuticals used in manufacturing. It would also create tax credits and grants for certain companies that build, expand, or convert facilities to make those products, starting for tax years on or after January 1, 2027. The law sets project cost limits, a $40 million yearly cap on tax credits, a $10 million minimum fund for grants, and a sunset date of December 31, 2036.

MO-2026-SB1586.s: The bill would change rules for solid waste sites and landfills. It would require a seller to tell the buyer and the state Department of Natural Resources if property has a solid waste disposal site or demolition landfill, and a buyer could cancel the sale if that notice is not given. It would also change how some fees are adjusted after October 1, 2027, and give the department more power to deal with abandoned waste sites.

MO-2026-SB1629.s: This bill changes rules for underground utility lines. It would require new and active underground facilities installed after August 28, 2026, to have a device that helps find them, unless they can be found above ground with an electronic tool. The rule would not apply to storm sewers, no matter how deep they are.

MO-2026-SB1652.s: The bill would create the Phoenix Alert System to help find abducted or missing African American women and girls. It would also set up a state office to work on preventing and ending that targeting, and it would require reports on its work each year. The bill would also create a fund for grants to community groups that help victims or work to prevent these crimes.

MO-2026-SB1694.s: The bill would expand Missouri's downtown and rural redevelopment program by allowing more types of tax revenue to be used for projects, loosening some rules on project areas, and changing how projects are approved and updated. It would also let some redevelopment projects run for up to 30 years. These changes would affect cities, developers, and others involved in downtown redevelopment projects.

MO-2026-SB834.s: The bill became law and sets new rules for mortgage changes and for sale-leaseback deals, where a person sells a home but stays on as a renter. It requires buyers in sale-leaseback deals to give the seller certain plain-language notices before the sale, and it lets the state attorney general or the seller sue for violations. For mortgage modifications, it says the loan still secures the debt, keeps its place in line, and is not treated as a new loan.

MO-2026-SB835.s: This law changes court rules and some insurance rules in Missouri. It says an insurer can keep the part of a property damage claim it paid, and it bars people from assigning certain post-loss insurance benefits for property damage, with some exceptions for lenders and later buyers. It also changes the Statewide Court Automation Committee, requires treatment courts without an administrator to hire one if funds are available, and adds three circuit judges in the 25th Judicial Circuit.

MO-2026-SB838.s: The bill would change several rules for electric utilities in Missouri. It would let electric transmission lines be placed in highway rights of way under set safety and review rules, and it would change how some renewable energy and battery storage power counts toward utility goals. It would also change rules tied to nuclear energy costs, utility surcharges, and zero-emission credit programs.

MO-2026-SB841.s: The bill would set several Missouri awareness days and months for health topics, including frontotemporal degeneration, blood donation, pediatric cancer, brain aneurysm, infertility, and PANS/PANDAS. It would also change rules for some municipal and hospital district hospitals, letting them invest more of their unused money and work in some of the same service areas. The bill would rename “epinephrine auto-injector” as “epinephrine delivery system” in state law and update rules for community paramedics.

MO-2026-SB863.s: Creates a new commission appointed by the governor to hear certain appeals about high school sports and other school activities. It covers decisions on student transfer eligibility for athletic reasons and on contests and contest rules. The state education department would support the commission, and its decisions would be final. Signed by the governor on July 9, 2026.

MO-2026-SB878.s: The bill would change rules for some pharmacy drugs and devices in Missouri. It raises the yearly limit on certain meth precursor medicines, sets a monthly fee for some manufacturers starting October 1, 2026, and changes how pharmacies can handle vaccines, medication therapy services, and medical device prescriptions. It also lets pharmacists dispense ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine without a prescription order if warning labels and approved procedures are in place.

MO-2026-SB890.s: The bill would require state departments that oversee an administrative body to send yearly reports to the General Assembly if that body has not met or done public work for three years. It would also move and rename the Division of Workforce Development and shift or end duties for several boards, councils, and advisory groups. These changes affect state agencies and the people who work with those groups; the bill was signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SB903.s: The bill changes Missouri rules on telecommunications infrastructure and related crimes. It updates the meaning of "critical infrastructure facility" and creates new crimes for damaging such a site or for having certain metals or fiber used in telecom systems without permission. It also makes some damage cases a class C felony and requires restitution and community service in some cases. The bill was signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SB904.s: The bill would change how Missouri treats hemp and some hemp-derived products. It would redefine industrial hemp, add a hemp definition, and treat intoxicating hemp-derived products as marijuana, which would limit production and sales to licensed marijuana-related facilities. It would also bar state agencies from sharing certain medical marijuana cardholder information, and it would let a customer ask a dispensary not to keep identifying records.

MO-2026-SB916.s: The measure would change when the state and its transportation department can be sued for injury or damage, including claims tied to motor vehicle use, unsafe property, and some project design, condition, or maintenance issues. It would also limit some claims against private contractors, subcontractors, engineers, and their workers on department projects, and it would bar contract terms that require them to defend or cover the state. It also changes how political subdivisions are treated when they buy liability insurance, and it was signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SB937.s: The bill would allow the state to transfer certain state-owned property in several Missouri cities and counties, including Harrisonville, Kirksville, Springfield, Festus, Doniphan, Higginsville, Jefferson City, Richwoods, Jackson County, Nodaway County, Marshall, Bowling Green, Joplin, and Potosi. It affects the state and the local areas named in the bill, and it has been signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SB938.s: The bill would raise the fee charged when a deed or other record is filed from $4 to $6. It would also change how that money is split, with $3 kept by the recorder of deeds, $2 sent to the Missouri Land Survey Fund, and the rest going to county general revenue. It would let the Department of Agriculture set fees for making or copying maps, plats, reports, studies, and other land survey records.

MO-2026-SB953.s: The law changes several water and environmental programs in the Department of Natural Resources. It changes how some fund balances are handled, updates the Clean Water Commission’s membership and conflict rules, and sets new rules for permits for some water contaminants. It also says people with rights to store water in a federal reservoir have the right to the return flow from that reservoir, subject to state rules and unused storage space.

MO-2026-SB959.s: Creates a Missouri geospatial advisory council inside the Office of Administration. The council would help the state keep a shared geospatial data system working and improving, and it would not be allowed to collect personal information about any person. Members would serve two-year terms. The bill was signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SB973.s: Missouri SB 973 became law and changes several rules for real estate deals. It removes some old waiting rules for unpaid property taxes, changes how land banks are run, and makes other updates to tax collection and sewer district rules. It also requires real estate wholesalers to give owners a written notice at least 14 days before a contract that transfers an interest in residential property, and owners may cancel if that notice is not given.

MO-2026-SB975.s: The bill changes how ambulance district board elections are set up, including letting county commissions use six election districts or an at-large election, and it lets districts change or end subdistricts through a public hearing and a two-thirds board vote. It also changes how board size changes, how vacant seats are filled, and how fast county commissions must hold hearings on annexation requests. The bill also sets new steps for ambulance district consolidation, including a required consolidation plan, public notice, hearings, and a process that can lead to consolidation if no objection is filed; it was signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SB984.s: The bill would change rules for pharmacy benefit managers and for audits of pharmacies. It would give pharmacies more notice before an on-site audit, limit how many prescriptions can be checked, and set new rules for when claims can be corrected and money taken back. It would also cap what people can be charged for some prescription drugs, require new contract and claim data rules, create a program for critical access care pharmacies, and set a date of September 1, 2028, for health plans to follow a federal law.

MO-2026-SB994.s: The bill would repeal several expired tax credits and make related updates to tax law for businesses, farmers, donors, and other taxpayers. It would extend the tax credit for donations of cash or food to certain groups until December 31, 2032. Starting January 1, 2027, it would let more military income be deducted from state taxes, add a new definition for the beginning farmer land-sale deduction, match state income tax return due dates to the federal date, and require more employers to file withholding returns online.

MO-2026-SB999.s: The law changes several rules about vulnerable people, including child protection, some criminal cases, and reviews of maternal deaths. It lets a prosecutor ask the Attorney General for help in some sexual offense cases, sets new rules for babies born alive during or after an abortion, and changes how the state review board studies and reports maternal deaths. It also changes rules for release from jail when a person has a no-contact order, and it was signed by the governor.

MO-2026-SCR21.s: This resolution encourages Missouri citizens to take part in patriotic programs and events for Show-Me America 250 on July 4, 2026, and throughout the year. It applies to people across Missouri.

MO-2026-SJR111.s: If approved by voters, this constitutional amendment would change how property tax rates are set in Missouri. It would remove the current break for taxes used to pay off debt, require local areas to set rates for each type of real property, and count new buildings and improvements when figuring tax values. It would affect counties and other local taxing areas.

MO-2026-SJR87.s: If approved by voters, this constitutional amendment would require each county to elect a sheriff to a four-year term by a majority vote. It would not apply to St. Louis City, St. Louis County, or St. Charles County. It would also require sheriffs to jail felons and traitors and let the attorney general seek removal through a quo warranto petition, which is a court filing to challenge someone’s right to hold office.

MO-2026-SJR95.s: If approved by voters, the measure would create the "Show-Me Prosperity Fund," a permanent state fund meant to support long-term budget stability. The fund would take money from state money set aside for it, plus gifts and grants, and the State Treasurer would invest it in stock index funds tied to the S&P 500. Money could not be spent from the fund until its investment earnings are enough to eliminate state taxes, and the fund would be limited to spending no more than 3% of its average value each year.

MO-2026-SRM1.s: A Senate resolution would formally object to Boone County Clerk Brianna Lennon. It affects that county office and election work.
